What must a Bloomington seller do before listing a house?

Before you list, show or sell a house in Bloomington, the city requires a Time-of-Sale housing inspection and a filed evaluation report. The rule covers single and two-family dwellings, condominiums, townhouses and mobile homes, and it applies to private sales as well, including a sale to a family member that is never listed. Multi-family rental buildings of four or more units are left out.

This requirement is the biggest difference between selling here and selling in most Minnesota suburbs, so it shapes the whole timeline. Cash buyers purchase as-is, but the city's inspection step still applies to the sale. The rest of this page walks through what the inspection costs, what it can force you to fix and who can take on a hazard.

How does the Bloomington Time-of-Sale inspection work?

The owner or listing agent schedules the inspection with the city's Building and Inspections Division at 952-563-8930 or through an online request form, and the evaluator needs about 120 minutes on site. The fee is $250, which includes the energy disclosure and any re-inspections, plus a service fee of $1.95 for an e-check or 2.95 percent for a card. If you cancel before a site visit, the city offers a refund of up to 50 percent within 60 days of your request.

  • The evaluator examines visible structure, heating, electrical and plumbing, and accessible attics and crawl spaces, and does not take anything apart.
  • The report does not cover lead paint, radon or asbestos, and it does not guarantee the home.
  • The report must be displayed at the house and given to the buyer before or at sale, and a copy must reach the city within 7 calendar days.
  • The report and the Certificate of Compliance are good for one year and only for the owner named on them.

Since April 2022 the inspection has included an energy disclosure covering the heating and cooling system, water heater, insulation and windows, and the city says no energy upgrades are required of the seller.

What counts as an immediate hazard, and who pays to fix it?

Only nine categories of defect must be corrected, and the seller is responsible unless the buyer agrees in writing to take them over. The city lists them as unsafe heating systems, unsafe water heaters, dangerous electrical conditions, unsanitary plumbing, structures unable to carry their loads, roofs, walls and foundations that are not weather tight, abandoned fuel tanks, unsanitary refuse or infestation, and missing or non-working smoke detectors.

Other defects are noted in the report but do not have to be repaired. If hazards are found, a re-inspection by a city inspector is required before the house can be occupied, and the owner or contractor must pull any permits. A buyer who is willing to take the hazards must get the city's written consent by signing a Hazard Correction/Responsibility form, which is currently handled through DocuSign by calling the same 952-563-8930 line. The Certificate of Compliance is typically required at closing.

Which sales are exempt from the Bloomington inspection?

Five kinds of transfer are exempt, but you must still call the city to say which exemption you are using. They are a newly built dwelling transferred to its first owner, a multiple dwelling already licensed as rental, a sale to a public body, a sale for demolition, and a sale by a sheriff or other court officer. The last exemption does not cover a sale by someone appointed by a probate court, which matters for heirs selling an inherited Bloomington house.

If your sale does not fit an exemption, plan for the inspection and the report date before you set a closing. Check any open work permits as well, because the owner or contractor must obtain the necessary permits and the dwelling is subject to re-inspection of open permits before occupancy.

What is Bloomington like, and who shops for homes here?

Bloomington is the largest suburb in the Twin Cities, with 89,034 people, 10 miles south of downtown Minneapolis on the north bank of the Minnesota River. It was settled in 1843, the Town of Bloomington was incorporated on May 11, 1858, and it became a city on November 8, 1960. The postwar housing boom filled in much of the street grid you see today.

Interstate 35W divides the city informally. West Bloomington is mostly residential with newer housing, while East Bloomington has more industry, retail and the less expensive housing. Highway 77 (Cedar Avenue), Highway 169 and Interstate 494 frame the rest of the map, and the Metro Blue Line light rail runs from the Mall of America to downtown Minneapolis and both airport terminals.

The employer base is strong. Mall of America tenants are the largest group, with Dayforce, Donaldson, Great Clips, HealthPartners and Toro headquartered here. ISD 271 runs fifteen public schools, with John F. Kennedy High School in the east and Thomas Jefferson High School in the west, and the attendance line runs near France and Xerxes Avenues. A buyer will ask which side of that line you are on.

Which city fees and bills should a seller check before closing?

Before closing, call the city to find out whether anything is owed on the property, because outstanding items are easier to clear before the title company asks. The city's Time-of-Sale page lists the right numbers.

  • Assessing Division: 952-563-8722, for fees or fines associated with the property.
  • Utility Billing: 952-563-8726, for the current outstanding water bill.
  • Environmental Health: 952-563-8934, for pending civil fines.
  • Finance: 952-563-4527, for pending weeds, trees, brush removal and abatements.

Hennepin County bills the property tax, due May 15 and October 15, and it takes recordings by appointment, online through its Virtual Recorder site with a $3 service fee, by mail or through eRecording for title companies. Its recording page lists a $46 fee per document and a $54 well disclosure certificate when one is needed, and it says properties with delinquent taxes cannot be transferred under Minnesota Statute 272.12. Minnesota Statute 513.55 separately requires a written seller disclosure before the purchase agreement is signed.

More questions about Bloomington, MN

Is the Bloomington inspection required for a cash sale?

Yes, it applies to any sale of a covered dwelling, cash or financed, listed or private. The only way out is one of the five exemptions in city code, and you still have to call the city to say which one applies.

Do I have to repair everything the Bloomington inspector finds?

No. Only the nine immediate hazard categories must be corrected, and the buyer can assume them with the city's written consent. Other deficiencies are listed in the report without a repair requirement.

How long is a Bloomington Time-of-Sale report valid?

One year from the date of issue, and only for the owner named on it.

Who gets the Certificate of Compliance?

The city sends it to the owner or listing agent once no hazards remain. It is typically required at closing, so ask your agent or title company to confirm they have it before the signing date.

Can an heir selling an inherited house in Bloomington skip the inspection?

Usually not. The sheriff and court-officer exemption does not apply to a sale by a person appointed by a probate court, so a personal representative should plan for the inspection and report.

Why is Lakeville, Minnesota, different from other Twin Cities suburbs for sellers?

Lakeville is the largest city in Dakota County and the ninth most populous in Minnesota, with 79,270 residents in the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate. It sits about 20 miles south of both downtown Minneapolis and downtown St. Paul along Interstate 35, and it grew 14.1 percent between April 2020 and mid-2025. That pace is the fastest of the four cities in the Census comparison, so sellers here deal with a market that keeps adding new homes alongside resales.

The city covers about 36 square miles of land. J. J. Brackett platted the town site in 1855 on a lake he called Prairie Lake; it was renamed Lake Marion after Marion Savage built the Dan Patch rail line to serve his Antlers Amusement Park in 1910. Lakeville was incorporated as a city in 1967 and stayed mostly agricultural until the interstate and rising metro land costs pulled housing south. Large farms growing corn, soybeans and dairy cattle still operate.

A branch of the Vermillion River, which the state has designated a trout stream, crosses Lakeville, and North Creek, one of its tributaries, starts in the northern part of the city. Winters are cold: weather-station data for 2010 to 2020 show a mean January daily high of 22.6 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of 10.4.

What do Census numbers show about Lakeville homes and households?

Lakeville has the highest home values and incomes of the four cities in the Census comparison. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $452,500 for 2020-2024, and 87.8 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, with 25,685 households averaging 2.89 people.

Do Lakeville rental and short-term rental rules affect a house sale?

Yes, if the house is currently rented or you are considering renting it first. Lakeville's council adopted a residential rental registration ordinance in September 2023 for long-term rentals, defined as 32 days or longer. Registration is mandatory, free, and one-time unless contact information or ownership changes, and the city does not require inspections. Owners of several rentals must file a form for each property.

Short-term rentals are allowed only with a Short-Term Rental Administrative Permit under Title 9, Chapter 10 of city code. Highlights from the city's list of requirements:

  • Listings must show the city permit number, maximum occupancy and maximum number of vehicles.
  • Overnight guests are capped at two adults per bedroom plus their dependent children.
  • Guest vehicles must park in the garage or on the driveway, and noise must be reduced between 10:00 PM and 7:00 AM.
  • Owners pay local lodging tax under Title 3, Chapter 17 of city code.

A buyer who wants to run a rental after closing will ask whether the property is registered, so file the registration if you still hold the house as a rental.

What are the ways to sell a Lakeville house on a short timeline?

Lakeville sellers usually weigh a full-service listing against a cash sale. With a median value of $452,500 and 87.8 percent owner-occupancy, most competing homes are single-family houses owned by their residents, so a well-prepared listing can draw several buyers in a city this size.

  • A listing makes sense when the house is current on maintenance and you can accept showings, appraisal timing and the buyer's financing conditions.
  • A direct cash sale fits a house with deferred repairs, a probate or inherited property, or a rental where the lease complicates showings.
  • Selling it yourself removes the agent fee but puts disclosures and negotiation on you.

Cold winters add one condition-related item: in January the mean daily high is only 22.6 degrees, so roof, furnace and insulation condition tend to draw buyer questions. Gather service records for those systems before you open the house to buyers. If the sale involves an inherited house, ask a title company whether the estate needs court paperwork before the deed can be signed.

Which Lakeville school district am I in, and why does it matter?

Most Lakeville households are in Lakeville Area School District 194, which runs two high schools, Lakeville North and Lakeville South, each with close to 2,000 students, plus nine elementary schools and three middle schools (Century, McGuire and Kenwood). Parts of northern and eastern Lakeville fall under District 196 (Rosemount-Apple Valley-Eagan) or Farmington District 192.

Because the boundaries date from the farming era, two neighbors can be in different districts. Minnesota's open enrollment law also lets families choose a school outside their home district. When you write your listing, name the exact district for the address so buyers do not have to guess.

Which employers, roads and areas draw buyers to Lakeville?

Airlake Industrial Park covers about 1,500 acres and holds as many as 200 companies with an estimated 4,500 employees. It is served by Airlake Airport, a reliever airport run by the Metropolitan Airports Commission. Post Consumer Brands has kept its headquarters in the city since 2015. The Minneapolis air route traffic control center sits a few miles away in Farmington.

Interstate 35 is the main artery, and Cedar Avenue (Minnesota Highway 77) runs along the east side. The Census puts the average commute at 23.6 minutes. The Argonne area, a post-World War I settlement project now covered with suburban retail, still appears by that name on maps.

How do I close the Lakeville water account and record the deed?

Lakeville bills residential water quarterly and calculates sewer charges from winter-quarter water use. The city's Form Center has an online stop-service form for sellers and a start-service form for buyers, and you can pay bills through InvoiceCloud, by mail, or at City Hall at 20195 Holyoke Avenue. Call the Utility Division at 952-985-2700 with questions about the meter.

Dakota County Property Taxation and Records records Lakeville deeds at its Hastings office. State deed tax of 0.0033 on a sale at the city's $452,500 median value comes to about $1,493. The county auditor must confirm there are no delinquent taxes before the deed can be recorded (Minnesota Statutes 272.12), and Minnesota Statutes 513.55 requires you to give the buyer a written disclosure of material facts before signing a purchase agreement.

Dakota County's 2026 tax calendar lists May 15 and October 15 as the due dates for the two halves of real estate tax. Late payments carry a 2 percent penalty on homestead property and 4 percent on other property under state law.

More questions about Lakeville, MN

How big is Lakeville compared with nearby cities?

Lakeville is the largest city in Dakota County, at 79,270 people in the 2025 Census estimate. Farmington next door has 25,425 and Inver Grove Heights has 36,873. Its size means a large pool of potential buyers and a lot of new construction competing with resales.

Do I need to register my Lakeville rental before selling it?

Lakeville requires registration of residential rentals of 32 days or longer, with no fee and no inspection. Register each property once, and update the city if ownership or contact information changes.

Can a buyer run a short-term rental in a Lakeville house?

Only with a Short-Term Rental Administrative Permit from the city, and the owner must follow the Title 9, Chapter 10 performance standards. Those include listing the permit number and limiting guests to two adults per bedroom.

How much deed tax will I see on a Lakeville sale?

State deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price above $3,000. On a $452,500 sale, that is about $1,493. Your title company will show the exact figure on the closing statement.

Who do I contact to stop Lakeville utilities when I sell?

Use the Finance forms on the city's Form Center to stop service, or contact the Utility Division at 952-985-2700. Bills are quarterly, so ask for a final read that matches your closing date.

Where is Blaine, and who buys homes there?

The city's own history says the population passed 75,000 by 2025, making Blaine the largest city in Anoka County. The count was 1,694 in 1950 and reached 70,222 at the 2020 count.

The land explains the housing. Sandy soil and wetlands discouraged farming, so dairy and sod farms later gave way to subdivisions. Developers in areas such as The Lakes and Club West dredged ponds and used the sand to raise the building sites, and Sunrise Lake in The Lakes is the largest water body in the city at 158 acres. Laddie Lake, at 77 acres, is the only natural lake.

Main routes are Interstate 35W, Highway 65, Highway 10, Highway 610, University Avenue, Lexington Avenue and Hamline Avenue. The National Sports Center opened in 1990 and the TPC Twin Cities golf course in 2000, and the sports center has more than 50 full-size soccer fields plus an eight-sheet ice arena.

Which school districts serve Blaine homes?

Three districts serve Blaine, and the one tied to your address is a real selling point. Anoka-Hennepin covers most of the city, including the area from Highway 65 to University Avenue north of 99th Avenue NE. Spring Lake Park Schools covers nearly everything south of 99th Avenue NE, and Centennial Schools covers the area east of Lexington Avenue and south and east of Interstate 35W.

The city has Blaine High School in Anoka-Hennepin, Centennial High School, and Paladin Career and Technical High School, a public charter school. Because boundaries run along streets and not neighborhoods, two houses a block apart can belong to different districts. Put the district name in your listing or your conversation with a buyer, and confirm it with the district before you quote it.

Set these values beside your own purchase price and loan payoff, and use the recent sale of a comparable house in your subdivision to test any offer.

Does Blaine require a rental license if I am selling a rental house?

Yes, Blaine licenses rental property every year, and a buyer who inherits your tenants takes on that duty. The city's application page lists a $190 fee for a single family rental, attached or detached, and $180 per building plus $10 per unit for multi-family. The license expires on December 31, and owners with three consecutive years without violations qualify for a reduced fee.

Single family rentals get an interior inspection every three years and an exterior inspection every year. For a rental sale, hand the buyer the license, the last inspection result and the tenant lease documents. An owner-occupied house that you are simply selling does not need any of this.

What happens at recording and closing in Anoka County?

Anoka County records the deed, and its rules decide whether the document is accepted. Its recording requirements page lists what a transfer deed must carry.

  • State deed tax of .0033 times the net consideration when the price is over $3,000, which matches Minnesota Statute 287.21.
  • A $5 agricultural conservation fee.
  • A completed electronic Certificate of Real Estate Value and its number on the deed.
  • A "Send tax statements to" line with the buyer's name and address.
  • Delinquent taxes paid in full before the transfer.
  • A well disclosure certificate with a $54 fee, or one of the two well statements the county prints on its page.

Anoka County also explains that Minnesota has two land record systems, abstract and torrens, and that most Anoka County property is abstract, so a title search should look for any documents tied to the lot. Your title company usually handles the filing, but you should know what the list asks for.

How are Anoka County taxes and the homestead handled when a house sells?

Residential homestead property in Anoka County is billed in two halves, due the middle of May and of October (the 15th of each), and the county notes that late payment brings penalties even if you never received a statement. The county's homestead rules add a point sellers miss: the owner must tell the assessor within 30 days if the home sells or stops being a primary residence, and the county can remove the homestead and impose penalties if no one does.

The county's page also says a Certificate of Real Estate Value is due at the auditor's office when a property sells, as Minnesota Statute 272.115 requires. A qualifying disabled veteran can receive a market value exclusion of up to $300,000 on homestead property, so buyers who are veterans may ask about it. Have the closing agent split the current half-year between you and the buyer by closing date.

What disclosures does a Blaine seller owe?

Before you sign a purchase agreement for a residential property, Minnesota Statute 513.55 requires written disclosure of material facts you know that could adversely and significantly affect a buyer's use and enjoyment. Section 144.496 adds a radon disclosure: whether tests were done, the latest reports, any mitigation system, a radon warning statement and the Minnesota Department of Health booklet.

The city sits on glacial sand, ponds and wetlands, so basement moisture is a fair thing to document. Gather any sump pump records, past repairs and test results before the first showing so the written disclosure is accurate and complete.

More questions about Blaine, MN

Which county records a Blaine deed?

Anoka County for most of the city. Blaine also reaches into Ramsey County, so confirm your parcel's county on your tax statement before sending any documents.

Do I need to pay deed tax when I sell in Blaine?

Minnesota's state deed tax is imposed on the deed and is calculated at .0033 of the net consideration above $3,000. Ask your title company who pays it under your purchase agreement, since the agreement decides that.

Is a rental license transferable to the buyer of my Blaine rental?

Check with Blaine Housing Services before closing. The license is issued yearly and expires on December 31, so the new owner should expect to apply for their own and schedule any inspection the city requires.

What if my Blaine house has radon or basement water problems?

Disclose what you know in writing. Minnesota law requires disclosure of known radon test results and of material facts that could significantly affect a buyer, and a seller who skips them can be held liable for damages.

How long does a Blaine house usually take to sell for cash?

It depends on the buyer and the title work, but a cash sale has no lender appraisal, so closing is often a matter of weeks. Anoka County's recording checklist is the main step that can delay a closing if something is missing.

Irish and German farmers claimed land here after the 1851 Treaty of Traverse des Sioux, and the township took its name from the Irish village of Inver and the German town of Grove. By 1880 there were 240 farms, four churches and four school districts. The village of Inver Grove and Inver Grove Township merged to form the city on March 9, 1965, and the population climbed from 6,266 in 1960 to 29,751 in 2000.

Notable local landmarks include District 7 School, Dakota County's first public school (1854), the 1894 Rock Island Swing Bridge, now a park, and the site where a B-52 bomber crashed on September 16, 1958. Southern Inver Grove Heights also holds the Pine Bend Bluffs Scientific and Natural Area, where a roughly 500 million year old impact crater was identified in 2022.

The final vote was expected after a November 10, 2025 reading. Ask the city clerk for the terms in force today if you are selling a house that is currently rented.

Rental licensing and vacant building registration are the two city programs a seller is most likely to meet.

  • An owner-occupied house with no code orders can be listed or sold directly with little city involvement.
  • A rental needs a current city license and a record of its inspection.

Work out which of the three describes your property, then read the matching section below.

What is Brooklyn Center, and what shapes its housing?

Brooklyn Center sits on the Mississippi River just north of Minneapolis and covers 8.4 square miles, of which 8.0 is land. The area was settled in 1852, formed a village from parts of Brooklyn Township and Crystal Lake Township on February 18, 1911, and became a charter city on December 8, 1966. Farmland was sold to builders in the 1940s, and the population reached 4,000 by 1950. Dayton's opened the Brookdale shopping center in 1960, when the city had passed 24,000 people.

The river is the eastern boundary. Upper Twin Lake (117 acres) feeds a chain of lakes that drain to Shingle Creek, the city has 26 parks and 20 miles of trails, and Palmer Lake Park preserves more than 200 acres of lake and marsh. The Heritage Center, the former Cap Martin estate that later passed to Earle Brown, is now a city-owned conference and event site. The main street, Brooklyn Boulevard, replaced the old Osseo Road route. Public schools are in Brooklyn Center Schools, ISD 286.

The city sits in plant hardiness zone 4b, where winter lows can reach minus 25 degrees, so heating, insulation and roof condition are worth documenting for a buyer.

Do you need a rental license to sell a Brooklyn Center rental?

You need one to operate the rental, and the buyer of a rental will ask to see it. Brooklyn Center has licensed rental property since June 1, 1975, and the rule covers any housing that is not owner-occupied, whatever the tax status or whether rent is charged. Short-term rentals such as Airbnb need a rental license too, but an owner-occupied house renting one or more rooms and approved accessory dwelling units do not.

In May 2026 the city adopted a two-year rental license. Every license is now issued for two years and must pass an inspection that uses city codes, the 2018 International Property Maintenance Code and applicable Minnesota codes. Operating without a license is a misdemeanor and can bring administrative citations and fines. If you are selling a licensed rental, give the buyer the license, the inspection results and the lease files and ask the city whether the buyer must apply for a new license.

What if the house is vacant when you sell?

Brooklyn Center requires a vacant building registration, and the fees climb the longer the house sits empty. Residential fees listed on the city's application, revised June 27, 2025, are shown below.

  • Single-family or townhome, vacant up to one year: $595 total ($195 re-occupancy inspection plus $400 registration).
  • Condo, up to one year: $515.
  • Duplex, triplex or fourplex under one owner: $675, $815 or $950.
  • Any residential type vacant one to three years: $1,000 a year.
  • Vacant more than three years: $3,000 a year.

The registration fee can be reduced by up to $300 if the property has no code violations, but you must call 763-569-3330 and meet the inspector on site before applying. The form says the first year of vacancy needs both the registration and a re-occupancy inspection, that sellers must tell buyers about correction orders, and that the buyer can take over responsibility for corrections by contacting the city. The ordinance's purpose is to protect neighborhoods from hazards and blight, and failing to comply is a misdemeanor.

How do utilities and special assessments work at sale?

Brooklyn Center bills water, sanitary sewer, storm drainage, street lights and recycling quarterly, and it generates a final bill when a property is sold. The city says final bills are produced several times a month. Delinquent utility bills are certified to property taxes each year as special assessments, with a $50 certification fee added, so a balance you ignore can follow the parcel onto the buyer's tax bill. The minimum residential bill for 2026 is $227.17 a quarter, or $174.43 with the senior sewer rate.

Special assessments for city projects are paid through the Community Development Department at 763-569-3330 before they roll over to county taxes. Ask that office for a payoff figure, and confirm it with your title company before the closing date.

Who handles assessing, taxes and recording for Brooklyn Center?

Hennepin County does all three, not the city. The county assesses the roughly 8,986 parcels in Brooklyn Center, sets estimated market value and classification, reviews each property in person every five years, and takes homestead applications at its assessor's office at 612-348-3046. A new owner has to file for homestead to receive the reduced taxable value, and the application asks for Social Security numbers of owners who live there and the Certificate of Real Estate Value.

Property tax is due May 15 and October 15, and Hennepin accepts payment online, by mail, at the Government Center or by direct payment. Taxes can be included in a mortgage payment through escrow. For recording, Hennepin County Recorder fees are $46 per document, a well disclosure certificate is $54, and an eCRV is required for deeds with taxable consideration over $3,000. Minnesota Statute 513.55 requires you to give a buyer written disclosure of material facts before the agreement is signed.

What does a vacant house cost to register in Brooklyn Center?

A single-family house vacant up to a year costs $595 in total. The fee rises to $1,000 for one to three years and $3,000 beyond three years, and up to $300 can come off the registration with a clean inspection.

Can a buyer take over code violations on a Brooklyn Center house?

Yes, the city's form says buyers can assume responsibility for corrections by contacting the city, and the sellers must tell buyers about correction orders. A buyer must also meet all city codes and the conditions of the approved property plan.

Is an Airbnb in Brooklyn Center covered by the rental license rule?

Yes. The city's rental page says short-term rental properties are required to hold a rental license. Renting out a room in an owner-occupied home is the exception.

Who do I call about homestead after I sell?

The Hennepin County Assessor's office at 612-348-3046 processes homestead for Brooklyn Center. The new owner files a homestead application with the Certificate of Real Estate Value, so give them the sale documents promptly.

Fridley licenses rental property, so a buyer who plans to keep the house as a rental should expect to apply for a license. The city uses two license subtypes: single family covers one to three units, and multi-family covers four or more. Applications go through the CitizenServe portal.

The owner must list a physical address, not a PO box. If the owner lives more than 50 miles from the property, a local contact is required. New owners can upload their purchase documents with the application because the owner shown in the portal comes from Anoka County records, which update every one to two months. Questions go to Fridley rental licensing at 763-572-3616.

If you are selling a rental and want the transaction to move smoothly, bring a copy of the current license certificate and any inspection results to the table.

How do I stop and transfer the Fridley water account at closing?

Tell the city's Utility Billing Division before your closing date, using the Moving In/Out form or by phoning 763-572-3529. Staff need a meter reading on the day of closing to prepare the seller's final bill, and the account switches to the new owner as of that date.

  • Residential water has a fixed charge of $26.01 per quarter plus tiered volume rates in the city's 2026 schedule.
  • Sewer is billed on winter-quarter water use, and recycling is $11.60 per quarter for homes.
  • Weekly garbage service comes from a private hauler licensed by the city, separate from the city bill.

Unpaid utility charges can become a lien and be sent to Anoka County to be collected with next year's property taxes. Notices go out on or before October 1 for balances billed through July 31. A 10 percent late fee can apply to past-due accounts.

What schools, roads and employers draw buyers to Fridley?

Fridley Public Schools, Independent School District 14, run Fridley High School, Fridley Middle School, Hayes Elementary and Stevenson Elementary. Parts of the city fall in other districts: a small northern area is in Anoka-Hennepin District 11, an eastern area is in Columbia Heights District 13, and much of the north-northeast belongs to Spring Lake Park District 16. Check the district for the exact address when you write the listing.

Interstate 694 and Minnesota Highways 47 and 65 are the main roads, and the Northstar commuter rail line stops at the Fridley station. The Medtronic operational headquarters, Unity Medical Center, a Target distribution center and the BNSF Northtown rail yard are among the larger employers and landmarks. Only about 21 percent of residents worked in the city in 2000, and the Census puts the average commute today at 22.6 minutes.

What does recording a Fridley deed cost in Anoka County?

Anoka County records Fridley deeds, and its fee schedule effective July 1, 2025 lists a $46 recording fee for abstract property, a $5 conservation fee and a $54 well certificate. State deed tax is 0.0033 of the net consideration over $3,000. On a sale at Fridley's $302,900 median value, that is about $1,000.

Property tax payments go to Anoka County Property Records and Taxation at 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, or online through PayAnokaCounty. The online system adds a 2.6 percent fee for cards and a $3.50 fee for e-checks, while checks and in-person payments at the Government Center carry no fee. State law splits the year's tax into two halves due before May 16 and October 16 (Minnesota Statutes 279.01), so the second half for 2026 has already come due.

Can I sell a Fridley house that has code violations?

Often, yes, but check the notice first. The city can add abatement costs to the property's taxes, and buyers often ask for credits. A cash buyer takes the property as-is, while a retail buyer may ask you to fix flagged items first.

Who do I call to close my Fridley water account?

Call the Fridley Utility Billing Division at 763-572-3529 before closing. The city needs a meter reading on the closing date, and the closing date ends the seller's account and starts the buyer's.

How much is deed tax on a Fridley home sale?

It is 0.0033 of the net sale price once consideration exceeds $3,000. At $302,900, that is roughly $1,000. Anoka County collects it with a $5 conservation fee when the deed is recorded.

Does the buyer of my Fridley rental need a rental license?

The city licenses rentals of one to three units and of four or more units, and a new owner applies through CitizenServe. The owner of record comes from Anoka County, so the application lets new owners upload purchase papers while that record catches up.

Do I have to disclose problems with my Fridley house?

Yes. Before you sign a purchase agreement, Minnesota Statutes 513.55 requires a written disclosure of material facts you know that could significantly affect a buyer's use and enjoyment of the property. The disclosure must be made in good faith.

How fast can you sell a house in Austin, MN?

Speed in Austin depends on the route you pick and on how clean the paperwork is. A cash buyer can close in a matter of weeks, while a listing runs on the buyer's lender and inspection calendar. Austin, population 26,689, is the seat of Mower County in southeast Minnesota, so most of the paperwork runs through the Mower County offices on First Street NE.

Before any buyer walks through, a seller can shorten the timeline by sorting out four things: the permit history of the house, the property tax status, any city charges tied to the parcel, and whether the lot sits in an area that flooded in the past. The sections below cover each of them with the Austin and Mower County rules in mind.

  • Sell on the open market and wait for financing and appraisal.
  • Sell privately to a neighbor, relative or investor and handle the paperwork yourself.
  • Accept a cash offer from a buyer who takes the house with every repair left to them.

What is Austin like, and who looks at houses there?

Austin is a meatpacking and healthcare town on the Cedar River, and its buyers are mostly local workers, first-time purchasers and investors. The town was platted in the spring of 1856, became a village in 1868 and a city in 1871. It grew around mills on the river, then around the butcher shop George Hormel opened in 1891, which became Hormel Foods.

Hormel is still the largest employer, and the city is known as SPAM Town USA because the corporate headquarters, a SPAM plant and the Spam Museum are all here. The Hormel Institute, a University of Minnesota cancer research center, is also in town. Austin Public Schools (ISD 492) and Riverland Community College are other large employers, and the hospital is part of Mayo Clinic Health System.

Geography matters for a seller as well. Austin is about 41 miles southwest of Rochester, 20 miles east of Albert Lea and 12 miles north of the Iowa line, with Interstate 90 on the east side. Those distances shape who answers a listing here: people tied to the plant, the hospital and the college, plus investors who look at small-town rents.

How do Austin's housing figures look?

Austin's typical owner-occupied home is valued at $163,900, far below the figures in the Twin Cities suburbs. The table lists the figures a seller is most likely to compare against an offer.

At $953 a month, median rent is low as well, which is why some Austin owners keep a house as a rental and others decide to sell it. If you are weighing that choice, the rental registration rules below are worth reading first.

Does a flood history affect selling a house in Austin?

Yes, it can, because many Austin homes were built in the Cedar River floodplain and buyers and lenders ask about it. The city's flood history lists major floods in July 1978, 1983, 1993, spring 2000 when the Cedar River crested at 23.4 feet, September 2004 and 2010. Dobbins Creek and Turtle Creek also run through town.

The city answered with buyouts. Flood-prone homes were purchased and demolished using a Community Development Block Grant and the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program, low areas were turned into parks, dikes were added after 2004, and a flood wall protecting downtown was finished in 2014. Should your lot be near the river or one of the creeks, ask City Hall at 500 4th Avenue NE for the parcel's floodplain status before you list, and ask your insurance agent what flood coverage costs.

Tornadoes are the other weather risk on record. An EF2 tornado crossed the northwest and north side of Austin on June 17, 2009. Roof age, siding and tree condition are the details a buyer's inspector will notice after a storm-prone stretch of years.

What permit and yard rules should an Austin seller check first?

Check your permit record first. The city's own FAQ warns that if you sell a building with modifications done without a permit, you may be required to tear the addition down, leave it unoccupied or pay for costly repairs. Permits are usually needed for additions, decks, garages, fences, pools, water heaters, re-roofing and electrical, plumbing and heating work.

Two routine ordinances also generate liens against sellers who ignore them.

  • Grass and weeds. City Code 10.13 sets an 8 inch height limit. After a notice from the weed inspector you have seven days to comply, then the city cuts it and certifies the cost to the Mower County Auditor as a special assessment collected like real estate taxes.
  • Sidewalk snow. Chapter 7.04 requires owners to clear public sidewalks within 12 hours after snow stops, and the city may clear them after 24 hours and bill the owner.

Deal with both before closing, since an unpaid assessment is collected the way real estate taxes are. Austin also does not allow chickens, which matters if you kept hens and a buyer asks about the coop.

Do Austin rental registration rules apply when you sell?

They apply if the house is a rental, and they can affect the buyer. Austin requires residential rental property to be registered under City Ordinance 4.29, and the city's rental program FAQ says a Change of Ownership form must be filed when a rental is sold. Ask the city whether the same tenants will stay with the new owner, because that decides which form is used.

If you live elsewhere for part of the year, the program also asks you to name a local rental manager who handles emergencies and inspections. Anyone planning to keep the tenants will want to see the rental registration and any inspection results, so pull those documents together before a deal is signed.

How do Mower County property taxes work at closing?

Mower County bills property tax in two halves, due May 15 and October 15, and second-half agricultural tax is due November 15. The Auditor-Treasurer's office is in the Government Center at 201 First Street NE, Suite 7, in Austin, and the phone is 507-437-9535.

  • The county does not mail second-half statements, so a buyer should ask for the amount.
  • Mail payments are judged by postmark, and a private postage meter mark does not count.
  • The county will not accept post-dated checks.
  • A missing statement does not excuse a late payment.

On the deed side, Minnesota Statute 287.21 sets the state deed tax at .0033 of the net consideration when the price is above $3,000, and the Hennepin County recorder's checklist adds that an eCRV is required for sales over $3,000 and that a deed cannot pass title while taxes are delinquent. A well statement or well disclosure certificate also has to accompany a transfer deed. Ask the Mower County recorder for the local filing steps and fees.

What must you tell a buyer in writing?

Minnesota Statute 513.55 requires a written disclosure of material facts you know before the purchase agreement is signed. It covers facts that could adversely and significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment of the property, made in good faith and to the best of your knowledge. A separate radon statute, section 144.496, adds a written radon disclosure and a copy of the Minnesota Department of Health booklet.

For an Austin house, the facts buyers care about most are basement water, past flooding, roof and furnace age, and any work done without a permit. Writing these down early keeps negotiations short, and it matters even more in a quick sale where the buyer is not hiring an inspector.

More questions about Austin, MN

Do I need an inspection from the city before selling in Austin?

Ask the building department at City Hall, 500 4th Avenue NE, whether any sale-time step applies to your address, and gather your permits and any rental registration so a buyer can see them.

What happens if I have unpermitted work on my Austin house?

A buyer may be able to require you to remove it, leave it unoccupied or pay for repairs. The city's FAQ says exactly that about modifications made without a permit, so ask the building office whether the work can be permitted after the fact before you list.

What are the due dates for Mower County tax?

May 15 and October 15, with second-half agricultural tax due November 15. The county does not mail second-half statements, so request the figure from the Auditor-Treasurer at 507-437-9535 if you need it for closing.

Can a high weed or grass notice block my sale?

It will not block the sale by itself, but unpaid mowing costs become a special assessment on the parcel. Austin allows 8 inches of grass and gives seven days after notice, so cut it early and ask the clerk for any pending charges.

Is Austin a good place to sell to a landlord or investor?

Often yes. Median rent is $953 and 71.5 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so investors look at the town. Registered rentals must follow Austin's rental ordinance, and a sold rental needs a Change of Ownership form filed with the city.

Roughly 14.6 square miles of land make up the city, which touches Lakeville on its west side, Empire Township on the east, and Castle Rock and Eureka townships to the south.

Locals split town along County Highway 50. The older downtown lies south of that road, where only a couple of large projects have gone in over two decades. North of it, subdivisions are newer, and a third growth area spreads east into Empire Township. A trail along the Vermillion River ties downtown, uptown and the Empire-side neighborhoods together, a feature worth mentioning in a listing or an offer conversation.

The city got its charter in 1872, making it the second-oldest community in Dakota County after Hastings. A fire on November 22, 1879 destroyed several houses, stores, a hotel and a grain elevator downtown. Growth came late: the 2000 count was 12,365, and by 2010 it had reached 21,086.

What do Farmington's housing numbers say about my sale?

The median owner-occupied home in Farmington is valued at $366,200 in five-year survey data covering 2020 through 2024, and 86.5 percent of housing units are lived in by their owners. A seller here is usually competing with other single-family houses, with few apartments in the mix.

Another number worth knowing: 29.1 percent of Farmington residents are under 18, the highest share among the four cities in that comparison, against 24.2 percent in Fridley and 20.8 percent in Inver Grove Heights. Families with children are a large part of the local population, which is worth keeping in mind when you describe the house. Owners without a mortgage report median monthly costs of $781, which is a useful benchmark when a buyer asks what it costs to carry the house.

How do I close out the Farmington city water account when I sell?

Call Farmington Utility Billing at 651-280-6883 before closing to book a final meter reading. The city does not shut water off when someone moves out, so the account keeps running until you close it.

  • Utility bills come quarterly, and the city bills water, sewer, storm water and street lights.
  • Trash and recycling are billed separately by Dick's Sanitation, which handles cancellations at 952-469-2239.
  • Any unpaid final utility bill is certified to the property as a special assessment, so a buyer's title company may hold money back at closing if the account is open.

Landlords selling a rental should know that Farmington keeps rental utility accounts in the owner's name, so the owner has to close the account, not the tenant. A late fee of 10 percent applies to rental accounts that fall behind. Ask Utility Billing for the exact balance on your closing date rather than estimating it from the last bill.

Which schools, roads and employers matter to Farmington buyers?

Farmington Area Public Schools, Independent School District 192, enrolls about 6,900 students. Its attendance area takes in Farmington, eastern Lakeville, and Castle Rock, Empire and Eureka townships. A Lakeville address can therefore sit in a different district, so confirm the district for the exact street before you write a listing.

Main routes are Minnesota Highway 3, Minnesota Highway 50, and Dakota County Roads 31 and 50. A federal air traffic control center for the upper Midwest operates here, and a Kemps packing plant is another long-standing employer. The Dakota County Fairgrounds, about 360 acres with gates on 220th Street and Highway 3, report the highest county fair attendance in the state.

  • Price point: the $366,200 median value compares with $452,500 in neighboring Lakeville.
  • Commute: the 27.7 minute average drive to work is long for the metro.

What are the quickest ways to sell a Farmington house?

Three routes exist: an agent listing, a sale handled on your own, or an as-is purchase by a cash buyer. Each one trades speed against price and effort.

  • Agent listing: strongest when the house shows well and you can ride out inspections and a buyer's loan approval.
  • Do it yourself: skips the commission, though marketing, forms and haggling fall to you.
  • Cash buyer: fits inherited houses, deferred repairs, tenant-occupied rentals and owners behind on payments, since the buyer accepts the house in its present state and the closing date can follow your schedule.

Whatever you choose, Minnesota Statutes 513.55 obliges you to hand the buyer a written disclosure of known material facts before a purchase agreement is signed. Condition questions differ by area: subdivisions north of County Highway 50 are mostly under twenty years old, while downtown houses are older.

What happens at the Dakota County recorder when a Farmington deed is filed?

The county's records office in Hastings handles every Farmington deed. Walk-in filing is by appointment at the Administration Center, and mailed packets go to 1590 Highway 55 in Hastings with a return envelope. Most parcels countywide are abstract property, so your title company will search the record before closing.

Minnesota's deed tax equals the net sale price times 0.0033. At Farmington's $366,200 median, expect about $1,208. A deed also has to carry a well disclosure certificate, or a line stating the seller knows of no wells (Minnesota Statutes 103I.235). Before a deed is accepted, the county auditor looks for delinquent taxes (Minnesota Statutes 272.12). Recording charges are fixed by state law and posted on the county's fee page, so your title company can quote the total.

When are Farmington property taxes due, and who pays at closing?

Dakota County bills in two installments, May 15 and October 15 in 2026, and the autumn one is now behind us. A missed half costs 2 percent on a homestead and 4 percent otherwise, with monthly additions through December (Minnesota Statutes 279.01).

Settlement statements normally split the current year's bill between buyer and seller by closing date. Check the county's parcel search for open balances ahead of listing. The next homestead application deadline is December 31.

If you owe back taxes, ask Dakota County Property Taxation and Records for the payoff amount. Keep your latest tax statement handy so you can confirm the parcel number and the amounts already paid.

More questions about Farmington, MN

How quickly can I close on a Farmington house?

A cash purchase can close on a date you choose, frequently within a few weeks, since no lender appraisal is involved. Listing with an agent generally runs longer. For either path, book the water meter reading with Farmington Utility Billing in advance.

Are repairs required before I sell in Farmington?

The disclosure statute asks for a written statement of material facts you know before a purchase agreement is signed, and it does not list required repairs. Cash buyers take the house as it stands. Retail buyers often negotiate fixes after an inspection.

What becomes of an unpaid Farmington utility bill after a sale?

It stays attached to the property. The city certifies unpaid water, sewer, storm drainage and street light charges as a special assessment, so buyers' title companies usually want the last bill settled. A final read keeps the number accurate.

Who files the deed for a Farmington sale?

Dakota County's records office in Hastings, normally through your title company. The state sets the fees, the deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price, and the deed needs either a well certificate or a no-wells statement.

Can I sell Farmington rental property while tenants live there?

Yes. Go over the lease terms with the buyer and your title company. Farmington keeps rental utility accounts in the owner's name, so plan to close that account on the sale date.
